attribution.note: Marcus's own summary of the Ruis et al. results, in his own post.

semantics.note: Faithfully keeps the task scope, the 80.6% figure and the 'most models' quantifier.

contract.note: Reading 80.6% as the template-averaged headline figure and 'most models' as most model families is an ordinary, fair reading. The 81.7% structured-prompt subset and the 82.8% single-template score are correctly set aside.

evidence.note: The original v1 preprint (2022-10-26) reports a best mean of 80.6% (text-davinci-002, k=30). Its size analysis shows flat or falling slopes, with only three families best at their largest size.

reviews.rationale: The original manuscript's headline best mean is 80.6%. The higher figures come from a prompt subset or a single template, which the contract excludes. Only Cohere, T0 and InstructGPT-3 performed best at their largest size, so most families showed little consistent gain from scale. Both parts hold.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: A near-analytic claim about how far the evidence of the time reached. The drafter's paraphrase keeps 'some measures' and the sufficiency claim.

contract.note: The plain reading (gains on selected measures did not establish that scaling suffices for AGI) is ordinary and fair. It does not turn the sentence into a forecast that scaling will fail.

evidence.note: The Chinchilla abstract (2022-03-29) shows a bounded research question about compute allocation. It shows the study's scope but makes no direct finding on sufficiency.
The BIG-bench paper (2022-06-09) says naive extrapolation to human-level performance depends on the limits of narrow benchmarks, which fits the claim's non-entailment point.

reviews.rationale: The scaling literature in the packet, as of the post date, measured bounded settings. BIG-bench explicitly warns that extrapolating benchmark gains depends on the benchmarks' limits. Nothing in the packet shows the improvements entailing that scaling suffices for AGI.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: A claim about the scientific status of scaling relationships. The paraphrase is faithful.

contract.note: Reading the claim as 'scaling relationships are empirical fits with no guarantee of continuing' is the ordinary, fair reading.

evidence.note: Kaplan et al. (2020) state they lack theoretical understanding of their scaling laws and that it is hard to know when the laws can be trusted.

reviews.rationale: The foundational scaling paper presents its laws as empirical relationships and gives explicit caveats about their theoretical basis and about extrapolation. The packet contains nothing that establishes a guaranteed law.

attribution.note: Marcus restates his own earlier prediction and stands by it.

semantics.note: An unqualified 'won't' with no deadline, so it is a scored forecast with an open horizon.

contract.note: The contract uses the post's own definition of scaling maximalism. With no deadline, requiring a validated AGI to contradict the claim, or an impossibility result to support it, is fair. AGI has no operational definition, so interpretation matters.

evidence.note: ARC Prize (2026-09-03) reports major progress by Astra but explicitly says it is not AGI. This is neither a contradicting AGI demonstration nor an impossibility result.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated and the packet shows no conclusive event. No independently validated AGI built through scaling exists, and no impossibility proof either. Elapsed time alone cannot settle the forecast.
